channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: It Is the Journey, Not the Destination: Moving From End Points to Trajectories When Assessing Chatbot Mental Health Safety
item.description: A King's College London and Aarhus team argues that prevailing safety suites score the last message of a scripted exchange, which misses how risk actually forms: over days or weeks of dialogue, through compulsive use, sleep disruption, withdrawal from human contact, and narrowing attention around the chatbot relationship. They propose treating the whole dialogue as the unit of analysis, reporting turn-by-turn delusion confirmation and harm enablement, and calibrating short tests against clinically realistic long sequences. They also argue transcript-only evaluation is insufficient, since similar language can reflect very different internal states, and call for consented transcript donation linked to health records so the field can move from anecdotes to denominators.

item.title: The Dynamics of Delusion: Modeling Bidirectional False Belief Amplification in Human-Chatbot Dialogue
item.description: Using a rare dataset of chat logs from people who exhibited delusional thinking, the authors fit a latent state model of accumulating and decaying influence and find that a bidirectional model substantially outperforms the assumption that humans alone drive the spiral. Humans exert strong but short-lived influence on chatbots, while chatbots exert longer-lasting influence on humans, and chatbot self-influence over its own future outputs is the dominant accumulated pathway. This is the first quantitative evidence that human and chatbot exchanges can form measurable feedback loops of delusion.

item.title: MindEval: Benchmarking Language Models on Multi-turn Mental Health Support
item.description: Designed with PhD-level licensed clinical psychologists, MindEval simulates realistic multi-turn therapy conversations and scores models automatically, with simulated patient realism validated against human text and judge scores correlated with expert ratings. Across twelve state-of-the-art models, all score below four out of six on average, with the sharpest weaknesses in AI-specific failure patterns such as sycophancy and overvalidation. Notably, reasoning ability and model scale do not guarantee better performance, and quality degrades with longer conversations and more severe symptoms, precisely the conditions under which vulnerable users engage.

item.title: DialogGuard: Multi-Agent Psychosocial Safety Evaluation of Sensitive LLM Responses
item.description: DialogGuard scores model responses in mental health and crisis settings along five high-severity dimensions: privacy violation, discriminatory behaviour, mental manipulation, psychological harm, and insulting behaviour, using a shared three-level rubric that human annotators and LLM judges can both apply. Benchmarked against human safety annotations, multi-agent judging beats single-agent scoring and non-LLM baselines, with dual-agent correction and majority voting giving the best accuracy and robustness, while debate raises recall at the cost of over-flagging borderline cases. The framework is released as open source with a web interface.

item.title: NeuroWise: A Multi-Agent LLM Glass-Box System for Practicing Double-Empathy Communication with Autistic Partners
item.description: Most autism communication tools train autistic people to accommodate neurotypical norms; NeuroWise targets the neurotypical partner instead, pairing a simulated autistic conversational partner with a stress visualizer, an interpreter that explains the partner's likely internal state, and a coach. In a between-subjects study with thirty adults, baseline chatbot users shifted toward blaming autistic deficits after a difficult exchange, while NeuroWise users moved away from deficit-based attributions and finished conversations in fewer turns. Participants rated the interpreter, not the coaching suggestions, as the most useful component, and the authors flag that autistic collaborators were not involved in design.

item.title: Large Language Models for Web Accessibility: A Systematic Literature Review
item.description: Surveying how LLMs are being applied to accessibility work, the review finds the field leans on general-purpose models and prompt-based interaction, with evaluation practice varying widely and rarely involving disabled users directly. Applications cluster on text-centric and structurally explicit tasks with WCAG as the dominant reference frame, while cognitive accessibility guidance receives little attention, a gap that matters most for neurodivergent and cognitively disabled users whose barriers are not markup problems.

item.title: Algorithmic Fairness: Challenges to Building an Effective Regulatory Regime
item.description: Proposed US federal and state laws increasingly mandate fairness testing, but this perspective argues they must first take a position on what fairness means, and experts still disagree, producing an expanding list of highly technical definitions that legislators are poorly placed to adjudicate. Several of these definitions are mathematically incommensurable, so a patchwork of jurisdictions adopting different standards invites inconsistent determinations about the same system. Existing anti-discrimination law adds a further layer, encoding conceptions of fairness that may not suit algorithmic evaluation at all.
